author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I receive no letters from you. I do not doubt that you love me no longer. I have sent you some newspapers, and several letters. I leave this very moment to pass the mountains.11 As soon as matters are settled I will send for you to come to me. It is the dearest wish of my heart. […]”
archive: Confidential Correspondence of Napoleon and Josephine (London, 1856) — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “My love, I have been at Calais since midnight. I think of setting out this evening for Dunkirk. I am satisfied with what I see, and am in very good health. I hope that the waters may benefit you, as much as the bustle, the sight of camps, and the ocean have me. Eugene has gone to Blois. […]”
archive: Confidential Correspondence of Napoleon and Josephine (London, 1856) — public domain
context: Calais: setting out for Dunkirk this evening.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “My love — I am deeply afiected by all that you say to me; but the season cold, the roads wretched, the region unsafe, I can not consent to expose you to such perils and dangers. Return to Paris, to pass the winter there. […]”
archive: Confidential Correspondence of Napoleon and Josephine (London, 1856) — public domain
context: Warsaw cold, roads wretched, region unsafe.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “My love — I am in the receipt of your letter. I have smiled at your fear for my safety. I am in despair at the tone of your letters, and at what I hear of you. I forbid you to weep, to be melancholy and anxious; I wish that you may be cheerful, amiable, and happy. NAPOLEON.”
archive: Confidential Correspondence of Napoleon and Josephine (London, 1856) — public domain
context: Smiled at her fears; despair at her tone.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Your letter of the llth, from Mayence, made me smile. I am, to-day, one hundred and twenty miles from Warsaw. The weather is cold but fine. Adieu, my love; be happy; have character. NAPOLEON.”
archive: Confidential Correspondence of Napoleon and Josephine (London, 1856) — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I send you a letter from General Darmagnac; he is a very good soldier, who commanded the thirty-second. He is much attached to me. If this Madame de Richemont is rich, and it would be a good match, I should see the marriage with pleasure. Introduce them to each other. NAPOLEON.”
archive: Confidential Correspondence of Napoleon and Josephine (London, 1856) — public domain
context: Darmagnac's letter forwarded; a good soldier.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I write you two words. I am very well. I am in movement to put my army into winter quarters. It rains and thaws as in the month of April. We have not yet had one cold day. Adieu, my love. Entirely thine. NAPOLEON.”
archive: Confidential Correspondence of Napoleon and Josephine (London, 1856) — public domain
context: Moving to winter quarters; rain and thaw.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I learn, my love, that the mischievous talk which was held in your saloon, at Mayence, is renewed. Silence it. I shall be much displeased if you do not find a remedy for this. You allow yourself to be afflicted by the remarks of those who ought to comfort you. […]”
archive: Confidential Correspondence of Napoleon and Josephine (London, 1856) — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “It is not right for you to go with humble equipage to the minor theaters. That is not suitable to your rank. You ought only to go to the large theaters in impsoing state. Live as you were accustomed to do when I was in Paris. My health is very good. The weather has changed to cold. […]”
archive: Confidential Correspondence of Napoleon and Josephine (London, 1856) — public domain
context: Humble equipage unworthy of her rank (×2 letters).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “My love — I write you a word. I have removed ray headquarters to a very pleasant chateau, something like that of Bessieres, where I have many fire-places. This is very grateful to me, as I rise often in the night. I love to see the fire. My health is perfect. […]”
archive: Confidential Correspondence of Napoleon and Josephine (London, 1856) — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “1 have your letter of the 5th of April. I see with pain that you are chagrined at what I said to you. As usual, your little Creole head becomes excited and afflicted, " tu petite tete Creole se monte et s'afflige" Let us then say no more about it. I am very well. […]”
archive: Confidential Correspondence of Napoleon and Josephine (London, 1856) — public domain
context: Her little Creole temper; chagrin read with pain.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I have received your letter. I do not understand what you tell me about ladies in correspondence with me. I love none but my little Josephine, good, pouting, and capricious, who knows how to quarrel with grace, as she does every thing else; […]”
archive: Confidential Correspondence of Napoleon and Josephine (London, 1856) — public domain
context: No ladies in correspondence with me.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I have received your letter of the 2d of May, in which I see that you are inclined to go to St. Cloud. I have seen with pain the bad conduct of Madame. Could you not speak to her to amend her life? Such conduct must soon draw upon her serious disagreements with her husband. […]”
archive: Confidential Correspondence of Napoleon and Josephine (London, 1856) — public domain
context: St. Cloud instead? Seen with pain.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I can appreciate the grief which the death of poor Napoleon has caused you. You can understand the anguish which I experience. I could wish that I were with you, that you might become moderate and discreet in your grief. You have had the happiness of never losing any children. […]”
archive: Confidential Correspondence of Napoleon and Josephine (London, 1856) — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I have received your letter of the 6th of May. I see in it already the injury which you are suffering; and I fear that you are not reasonable, and that you afflict yourself too much from the calamity which has befallen us. Adieu, my love. Entirely thine. NAPOLEON.”
archive: Confidential Correspondence of Napoleon and Josephine (London, 1856) — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I have received your letter of the 10th of May. I see that you have gone to Lucken. I think that you may rest there a fortnight. That will give much pleasure to the Belgians, and will serve to divert your mind. I see with pain that you are not wise. Grief has bounds which it should not pass. […]”
archive: Confidential Correspondence of Napoleon and Josephine (London, 1856) — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I have received your letter of the 16th, and see with pleasure that Hortense has arrived at Lucken. I am, indeed, grieved by what you tell me of the state of stupor in which she still continues. She should have more fortitude and should govern herself. […]”
archive: Confidential Correspondence of Napoleon and Josephine (London, 1856) — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I am very well, my love. Your letter of yesterday gave me much pain. It appears that you are continually sad and that you are not reasonable. The weather is very bad. Adieu, my love; I love you and desire to hear that are cheerful and contented. NAPOLEON.”
archive: Confidential Correspondence of Napoleon and Josephine (London, 1856) — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “A have received, my love, your letter of the 3d of December, in which I perceive that you have been much pleased with the Garden of Plants. I am now at the most distant point of my journey. It is possible that I may soon be in Paris, where I shall be most happy to see you. […]”
archive: Confidential Correspondence of Napoleon and Josephine (London, 1856) — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I have received, my love, your letter. I see with pleasure that you are well. I have just come from a drive over the battle-field of Jena. We breakfasted upon the spot where I passed the night in bivouac. I have been present at a ball in Weimar. The Emperor Alexander danced. […]”
archive: Confidential Correspondence of Napoleon and Josephine (London, 1856) — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “My love — I arrived here yesterday at two o'clock in the morning: I came in order to see my troops. My health was never better. I know that you are well. I shall be in Paris at a moment when nobody expects me. Every thing goes well here, and to my satisfaction. Adieu, my love. NAPOLEON.”
archive: Confidential Correspondence of Napoleon and Josephine (London, 1856) — public domain
context: Kems, 2 a.m.: come to see the troops.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “My love — I have received two letters from you. I write to Eugene. I have ordered that the marriage should take place between Tascher and the Princess of Leyen. I shall go to-morrow to Antwerp to see my flotilla, and to direct the works. I shall be on my return the 15th of May. […]”
archive: Confidential Correspondence of Napoleon and Josephine (London, 1856) — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “My love — I have received your letter of the 3d of July. You will have seen Eugene, and his presence will have done you good. I have learned with pleasure that the waters agree •with you. […]”
archive: Confidential Correspondence of Napoleon and Josephine (London, 1856) — public domain
context: Eugene's presence will do her good.

author: Duke of Wellington
displayText: “A Public Man's Duty. It is necessary for a man who fills a public situation, and who has great public interests in charge, to lay aside all private considerations, whether on his own account or that of other persons.”
archive: Wellington, Despatches 1799–1815 (1902 selection) — public domain

author: Duke of Wellington
displayText: “Foundation of Discipline. The foundation of every system of discipline which has for its object the prevention of crimes, must be the non-commissioned officers of the army.”
sourceTitle: To To the Earl 0/ Liverpool, Fuente Ouinaldo, 1812-06-10

author: Duke of Wellington
displayText: “False Repobts. Tou are quite right to put no faith in reports from the coast of France. There are more false reports in France than even in Spain. In fact between the Government, and those who detest the Government, there is no truth in France. I have been told twenty times thaf 9o WORDS OF WELLINGTON. […]”
sourceTitle: To To Col Btmbnry, Under Secretary of State, Seysses, 1814-04-01

All are at times to a certain degree exposed to it; and I perfectly recollect seeing the Household Brigade at one time in a situation in the pursuit in which they were so. […]”
sourceTitle: To To Col Torrens, Military Secretary, Seysses, 1814-04-01

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I intend to use all haste with the commissions for your wife. Desiree demands my portrait; you will give it to her should she still wish for it; this not being the case, keep it for yourself. […]”
sourceTitle: To Joseph Buonaparte, Prairial 1795 (revolutionary date; day approximate)
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Prairial Year III: Désirée demands his portrait. Revolutionary calendar date; rendered to the 1st, marked approximate.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “My Friend, — I have not received any news from you for several days; I should, however, have been glad to know what effect the waters have had, and how you pass your time. I have been here for the last week, and intend going to-morrow to Boulogne. […]”
sourceTitle: To Josephine, Nivose 1804 (revolutionary date; day approximate)
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Nivôse Year XII: no news for days. Revolutionary calendar date; rendered to the 1st, marked approximate.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I see with pleasure that you are ready to sail. Your arrival in the Mediterranean is all the more important because the English are preparing to reinforce their army at Aboukir. […]”
sourceTitle: To Admiral Bruix, Prairial 1801 (revolutionary date; day approximate)
